content: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) refers to disorders of the heart and blood vessels, including coronary artery disease (CAD), heart failure, arrhythmias, and stroke. South Asians (people with ancestry from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, and the Maldives) are recognized as having a disproportionately higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared to many other ethnic groups. This increased risk is multifactorial, including genetic predispositions, unique metabolic profiles such as insulin resistance and central obesity, and lifestyle factors. The term “South Asian cardiovascular risk” encompasses this complex set of causes leading to early onset and more severe forms of CVD. Mechanistically, South Asians tend to have increased prevalence of metabolic syndrome, diabetes mellitus type 2, elevated lipoprotein(a), and dyslipidemia characterized by low HDL (high-density lipoprotein) cholesterol and high triglycerides. These factors accelerate atherosclerosis, leading to coronary artery disease and stroke. Clinically, South Asians may present with symptoms such as chest pain (angina), shortness of breath, palpitations, or may be asymptomatic and diagnosed on routine evaluation. Evaluations include risk scoring, lipid panels, blood sugar testing, imaging such as echocardiography, and stress testing. Management requires a combination of pharmacologic (e.g., statins, antihypertensives) and lifestyle interventions focusing on diet, physical activity, and smoking cessation. Important practical considerations include culturally appropriate dietary advice, recognition of the higher baseline risk, and tailored preventive strategies. While much evidence on CVD derives from broader populations, South Asian-specific research is emerging but still relatively limited, necessitating cautious extrapolation of guidelines. Safety considerations involve the risks of medication side effects and the need for long-term adherence. Understanding the unique aspects of cardiovascular disease in South Asians is essential for improving outcomes in this high-risk group. Major synonyms and related terms include coronary artery disease (CAD), ischemic heart disease, heart disease in South Asians, and South Asian metabolic risk. Limitations include variability within South Asian subgroups and evolving evidence base. This summary aims to support improved consumer health literacy and personalized care.

chunk_title: Epidemiology and Risk in South Asians
content: South Asians exhibit disproportionately higher rates of cardiovascular disease compared to other ethnic groups. Studies demonstrate an increased prevalence of CAD, with up to twofold higher risk of myocardial infarction (heart attack). The INTERHEART study and other large cohorts have shown South Asians experience heart disease at younger ages and with fewer traditional risk factors, implicating unique underlying mechanisms.

content: Genetics in South Asians contribute to heightened cardiovascular risk. Traits such as higher levels of lipoprotein(a), low HDL cholesterol, and increased insulin resistance are more common. Metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes and central obesity (abdominal fat) are prevalent, further increasing risk. These factors promote atherosclerosis, the buildup of fatty plaques in arteries, which underlies many cardiovascular events.

content: Traditional risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, and diabetes are common in South Asians. Emerging risk factors include increased inflammatory markers, elevated homocysteine levels, and prothrombotic states. Socioeconomic and psychosocial stressors, as well as diet and physical inactivity, also contribute. These factors may cluster in metabolic syndrome, more frequent in South Asians, amplifying cardiovascular risk.
